5	sometimes fail to improve strength or performance, as is commonly the case among elite athletes. 
6	In this 
7	situation, it may be necessary to disrupt the persistent state of stagnation by use of one of the following shock 
8	methods (see 7.1):
9	• plyometrics 
10	• forced repetitions
11	• supramaximal methods 
12	• electrical stimulation (macrostimulation)
13	• repeated single I RM training 
14	• restricted range maxima
15	• contrast methods 
16	• maximal eccentrics
17	The appropriate method, its timing and the duration of its use must be chosen with great care, since lack of 
18	progress may be due to overtraining rather than long-term stagnation. The use of any shock method under such 
19	circumstances is potentially harmful and definitely detrimental to performance. These methods arc generally 
20	unsuitable for novices and should only be employed by experienced athletes with a solid background of special 
21	strength training.
22	5.2.5 The D evelopm ent of Strength-Endurance
23	Strength-endurance involves the production of muscular tension without a decrease in efficiency over a long 
24	period. Strength-endurance, like explosive strength, has several forms, depending upon the motor pattern of the 
25	athletic activity, in particular the categories of dynamic and static endurance.
26	Dynamic strength-endurance is typical of exercises involving repetitive and significant muscular tension at a 
27	relatively slow speed of movement, as well as repeated cyclic or acyclic exercises requiring speed-strength. In the 
28	latter case we are referring to the specific endurance to execute special speed-strength and explosive work without 
29	adecrease in efficiency over a relatively long period. Static strength-endurance is typical of activities associated 
30	with the maintenance of maximal and near-maximal tension, as well as the moderate tension necessary for holding 
31	a specific posture (for example, in shooting or speed-skating).
32	The development of strength-endurance is an inherent characteristic and a fundamental principle of training 
33	for dev eloping general endurance. Training for strength-endurance is determined predominantly by:
34	1. The magnitude of the load
35	2. The tempo of movement
36	3. The duration of each movement and each phase of the movements
37	4. The rest interval between training sessions
38	5. The length of the training period
39	6. The initial levels of strength-cndurance of the athlete
40	7. The kinesiological structure of the movement
41	8. The relative involvement of static and dynamic strength-endurance.
42	Repetition work with weights 25-50% of IRM at a moderate tempo (from 60-120 repetitions/minute) is used for 
43	developing strength-endurance. The effectiveness of strength-endurance development, using equivalent weights 
44	and movement tempos, will be higher if the work is executed to complete fatigue, although work of shorter 
45	duration (60% of the maximal work capacity time) also will yield satisfactory results (Agolinsky, 1953; 
46	Korobkov, 1953; Monogarov, 1958; Diachkov, 1961).
47	Strength-endurance, like the other characteristics of muscular activity, is specific. However, the specificity 
48	of strength-endurance is expressed to a lesser degree than the specificity of speed, for example, while its carry­
49	over from one activity to another is greater. When the activity involves repetitively overcoming significant 
50	resistance (exceeding 75-80% of IRM), one cannot enhance endurance, since one becomes constrained to 
51	developing strength predominantly (Zatsiorsky, 1966).
52	This study by Zatsiorsky showed that isometric endurance increased 84% as a result of exercising 10 times a 
53	day for 5 weeks with the elbow flexors holding a 60% maximal contraction for as long as possible. Dynamic 
54	auiurance increased by 93% as a result of performing these arm curls with a weight of 60% of 1 RM at a rate of 
55	28repetitions per minute until it was impossible to increase the tempo further. At the same time, the ability to 
56	execute repetitive isometric contractions (60% of maximal strength for 5 seconds of tension and 2 seconds of rest) 
57	to failure increased by 219%. A similar experiment with 10 dynamic movements executed daily with maximal 
58	resistance for 5 weeks resulted in increases in both dynamic and static strength, but dynamic and static endurance
59	285
60	
61	######## PDF 297 (printed 286)
62	SUPERTRAINING
63	remained almost unchanged (Hansen, 1963). This indicates that it is necessary to optimise the volume of work 
64	required to develop strength-endurance.
65	It has been established that an increase in strength-endurance contributes to improving endurance in distance 
66	runners, skiers and skaters (Popov, 1968; Nabatnikova, 1972; Mikhailov & Panov, 1975). However, it must be 
67	emphasized that the magnitude of the strength load used is different if, on the one hand, the key quality required 
68	is general endurance and, on the other hand, it is strength-endurance.
69	It should be noted that certain popular strength exercises such as running with a sack of sand weighing 25% of 
70	the subject's bodyweight, barbell pressing, squats, 'good mornings', and twisting with a barbell not only do not 
71	enhance, but to a certain degree, will even hinder the development of endurance in cyclic type exercises 
72	(Maisuradze, 1960). It some instances the increase in strength is associated with excessive muscle hypertrophy, 
73	which is a by-product of strength training. Endurance and hypertrophy do not increase simultaneously and there 
74	is no correlation between them (Maison & Broekcr, 1941; McMorris & Elkins, 1954).
75	The lack of a definite correlation between special strength and muscle mass in different sports where the key 
76	quality is endurance has been observed by several authors (Chistyakov, 1965; Chcmyaev, 1965; Nabatnikova, 
77	1972). This conccms primarily cyclic sports (middle distance running, skating and skiing). In other cases, for 
78	example, with gymnasts, a positive linear correlation (R = 0.77) is noticed between strength-endurance and 
79	relative strength (Zhalei, 1964). Therefore, in those cases where endurance is associated with the display of 
80	significant strength, some muscular hypertrophy does not negatively influence training results.
81	The general principles concerning the development of strength-endurance, which were discusscd earlier, arc 
82	applied differently in each specific case, depending on the characteristics of the sport, for example:
83	• During the preparatory period, skiers should exercise with weights which are up to 65% of 1RM, in 
84	combination with simulation exercises on a flat surface, as well as with movements on roller-skis 
85	(Chistyakov, 1965).
86	• Middle and long distance runners obtain good results from lifting a barbell of 55-60% of bodymass up to head 
87	level 8-10 times rhythmically, clean-and-jerks with various weights (60-85% of bodymass); jumps with 
88	kettlebells from a squat position (using about one-third of bodymass for 18-20 repetitions) and squats with 
89	55-60% of bodymass until complete fatigue (Likachycvskaya & Kovalchuk, 1963). Exercises with weights 
90	of 60-80% of 1RM for multiple repetitions, jumping and hard running are also recommended (Popov, 1966).
91	• Exercises with heavy weights (80-85% of 1RM), as well as medium and small weights are recommended for 
92	developing strength-endurance in skaters. Exercises with heavy loads are executed for several sets at a 
93	moderate tempo for 4-12 repetitions per set until the point of complete fatigue, with 2-4 minutes of rest 
94	between sets. Exercises with light and moderate weights are executed as rapidly as possible for 15-25 
95	repetitions per set, for 3-5 sets with rest intervals of 5-8 minutes (Mikhailov & Panov, 1975).
96	• Male rowers obtain good results with weights of 50-80% of 1 RM and female rowers with loads of 30-40% of 
97	1RM (Ulrich ct al, 1966). Significant improvement (up to 40% from initial levels) in strength-endurancehzs 
98	been noted in women rowers working with light weights (18-20kg) for many repetitions (Chumakova, 1964). 
99	Improvement is greater with these weights than with larger loads (35-50 kg) executed in sets of 2-3 
100	repetitions, and it is even greater (by 28%) than that produced by a combination of both methods.
101	It is necessary to increase the amount of weight and the number of repetitions as strength-endurance increases. 
102	The following method is recommended for skaters to develop strength-endurance in the legs: increasing the 
103	number of barbell squats by 20-30 each week (beginning with 50 squats per set and over a period of 2-3 months 
104	increasing this to 200-300 repetitions), then increasing the amount of weight and starting a new cycle of strength 
105	training, but beginning with a smaller number of squats (Mikhailov & Panov, 1975).
106	For developing strength-endurance it is always appropriate to strive to execute the work under demanding 
107	conditions, though with movements whose coordination and structure in space and time are close to those of the 
108	special exercise. For instance, a runner may run with a small parachute resisting him or pull a loaded sled in the 
109	preparatory phases (Popov, 1966). Similarly, gymnasts may use a heavy belt and vest (Zhilei, 1964) and rowers 
110	a spccial water-resistancc dcvice attached to the hull of the boat (Chuprun, 1966). In the case of the rowers. 
111	strength-endurance as measured by the number of pull-ups, the number of arm flexions in the prone position and 
112	the number of barbell presses in 30 seconds increased by 57.1%, 27.8% and 9.1%, respectively.
113	286
114	
115	######## PDF 298 (printed 287)
116	SUPERTRAINING
117	Thus, multiple repetition exercises with various weights should be considered the fundamental method for 
118	developing strength-endurance, with the load being determined by the dynamics of the given exercise. In cases 
119	requiring intense effort, an optimally heavy weight should be used together with light weights or with exercises 
120	simulating the given sport activity. If the special exercise is associated with the prolonged production of moderate 
121	force, then it is useful to work with light weights in repeated sets to the point of fatigue or failure.
122	Strength training should not result in increased muscle mass in those types of sport where the key quality is 
123	endurance of moderate work output. If strength-endurance is required, especially in those cases where it is 
124	necessary to overcome a large resistance, a small increase in muscle mass is permissible. In no cases, should the 
125	training ever produce a decrease in relative strength of any muscle groups in the body.
126	5.3 Application of Special S trength Training Means
127	The value of systematic application of the training means has been investigated repeatedly, but the preliminary 
128	conclusions still need to be extended. Consequently, there have been attempts to devise a rational combination of 
129	strength, speed and endurance exercises to:
130	• raise the body's general work capacity (Zimkin, Yakovlev, Korobkov, Zatsiorsky )
131	• investigate the effectiveness of sequential and concurrent (parallel or complcx) use of the means for 
132	developing endurance and speed-strength (Ozolin, Diachkov, Mikhailov, Volkov ct al)
133	• study the effect of the sequential use of aerobic and anaerobic exercise on the development of endurance 
134	(Volkov ct al, Gordon et al)
135	• investigate the sequential use of strength and speed-strength exercises as one of the schcmes for 
136	systematically developing explosive strength (Ozolin, Diachkov, Vorobyev, Filin, Vcrkhoshansky).
137	However, research in the area of the systematic use of means is limited and no definitive practical 
138	recommendations have yet emerged.
139	The systematic use of means of special strength training over a given period produces a cumulative effect 
140	which is significantly greater than the separate non-sequential application of these same means. In principle, there 
141	at two possible variants for the systematic application of means: sequential and concurrent, as mentioned above:
142	1. The first variant (sequential means) involves the strictly determined, successive introduction of different 
143	means, each with a higher training effect, into the annual or multi-annual cyclc. The theoretical basis for this 
144	variant is based upon two observations:
145	• the training effect of any means diminishes as the body adapts to its influence
146	• the training effect must be maintained by using a complcx of means to steadily increase the body's special 
147	work capacity.
148	In addition, experience and research indicate that the training regime designed to develop a particular motor ability 
149	is determined largely by the degree of continuity in sequentially changing means with different training effects. 
150	Because of this, functional changes produced by earlier means should create favourable conditions for achieving 
151	the training effect of subsequent means. To devise a systematic sequence of the means of special strength 
152	training, one must:
153	• assess the quantitative and qualitative components of the training effect
154	• categorise the means relative to the level of the athlete's special fitness.
155	This, in effect, is the subject of research aimed at identifying the principles for devising logical systems for 
156	applying the different means of special strength training effectively. As an example, the sequential development of 
157	endurance begins by training aerobic (cardiorespiratory) processes, then non-oxidative glycolysis and finally high 
158	energy phosphagen processes. This sequential introduction of'anaerobic' work creates favourable conditions for 
159	the training effect of'aerobic'work (Ozolin, 1959, 1970; Volkov, 1963; Yakovlev, 1957; Borisov, 1979).
160	2. The second variant (concurrent means) involves the parallel use of means (over an extended period) that are 
161	close to the body’s work regime, but which produce a largely different training effect. This method is based on 
162	experimental evidence that adaptation elicited by the separate components of the complex of training work is not 
163	amply a summation of the separate effects, but the synergistic result of the interaction of the effects at each stage 
164	of training. This interaction produces a new physical state with a significantly greater work potential than would
165	287
166	
167	######## PDF 299 (printed 288)
168	SUPERTRAINING
169	have resulted from the separate non-systematic use of these same means, even at increased volume. Experimental 
170	assessment of the cumulative effects of different variations of the combination of means is necessary for applying 
171	the complex system of special strength training means.
172	A number of researchers, including Purvin, FChodykin, Dcniskin, Tatian and Chemousov have studied the 
173	systematic use of special strength means in speed-strength sports. They have established that the sequence of 
174	means in the preparatory period (beginning with strength, then speed-strength means, or vice-versa) has no real 
175	significance for novices. Consequently, the same effect can be obtained by using these means in any order.
176	A relatively larger effect than produced by the above-mentioned variants (with the same volume of training 
177	load) occun-ed in groups who used strength and speed-strength means concurrently by alternating them in mixed 
178	training sessions. This alternation sequence creates the optimal conditions for functional adaptation. This docs 
179	not ignore the fact that this training regime, with a rest interval between sessions on the same day, also produces a 
180	positive response of the after-effect phenomenon by use of the strength and speed-strength exercises. On the 
181	whole, this elicitcd more intense and more stable adaptation. It should be noted that the contrasting of stimuli in 
182	mixed workouts by alternating training means which are primarily of a strength and speed-strength character 
183	undoubtedly has a positive effect.
184	In another experiment one group of novice athletes used weights exercises in the first stage of training and 
185	plyometric depth jumps in the next stage. A second group did the same exercises in reverse order and a third 
186	group did these same exercises together in both stages, although not in the same workout. It was established that 
187	the first variant was more effective for developing speed-strength. The concurrent use of exercises (the third 
188	variant) caused significant improvement in speed-strength in the first stage, but the rate of improvement in speed- 
189	strength decreased noticeably in the second stage, due to monotonous repetition. The second variant (reversed use 
190	of these same means) produced significant improvement after the first stage due to the larger training effect of the 
191	plyometric method. However, the acquired speed-strength qualities were lowest at the end o f the second stage.
192	Another experiment studied the question of whether the execution of speed-strength exercises in one workout 
193	against the background of the positive after-effect produced by previous tonic strength work influences the 
194	effectiveness of speed-strength preparation of novices. One group of athletes executed exercises in this sequence 
195	(i.e. strength, then speed-strcngth work) during the fundamental stage of their workouts, while another group did 
196	the reverse. The pauses between exercises were increased slightly to minimise the influence of the positive after­
197	effect of the preceding work on the subsequent work. A third group executed depth jumps. The presence of this 
198	group in the experiment served two purposes: firstly, to study the effectiveness of plyometrics and secondly, to 
199	compare this effect with the results obtained with a complcx of less effective means. There was no statistically 
200	significant difference in speed-strength of the subjects in the first two groups. The largest increase in all the 
201	parameters of the control movement was discovered in the third group.
202	Thus, an increase in the training effect of speed-strength exercises performed against the background of the 
203	positive after-effect of strength work has not been corroborated in the training of novices. In this experiment, the 
204	means with a higher training effect (i.e. dcpth-jumps) produced significantly larger improvement in speed-strength 
205	fitness for a smaller volume of training. In explaining these results, one should take into account that any training 
206	influence will leave significant traces in an untrained person. The body is unable to react selectively to a chiefly 
207	strength or speed-strength means in one workout. In addition, the period over which the traces of the training 
208	stimulus are maintained is apparently longer than the duration of the after-effect of prior tonic work. Within one 
209	workout, the traccs of all the training tasks arc summed, which results in the same effect, despite these tasks being 
210	done in succession.
211	These findings should not be considered to disprove in general the appropriateness of using a complex of 
212	means in training, which exploits the positive after-effect of preceding strength work to enhance the training effect 
213	of the subsequent speed-strength and speed work. Since the experiment was conducted on a group of novice 
214	athletes, it is very likely that their lower level of special fitness excluded the possibility for exploiting this 
215	phenomenon adequately. A well-trained athlete can expect the preceding strength work to have a positive effect 
216	on the training effect of speed-strength and speed work in a training programme. However, the validity of this 
217	hypothesis can be established conclusively only by careful experimentation.
218	In an experiment with junior class sprinters the specific effect of short jumping exercises and the systematic 
219	use of combinations of these exercises was investigated. The jumping exercises involved variations of repeated 
220	jumps on one and two legs, as well as variations of triple and quintuple standing broad jumps and long jumping 
221	exercises (multiple jumps on one leg or from leg to leg over distances of 30- 100m). One group of sprinters 
222	executed mainly short jumps, a second group did mainly long jumping exercises and a third group did both fora
223	288
224	
225	######## PDF 300 (printed 289)
226	SUPERTRAININC
227	period of eight months (see Fig 5.12). The short jumping exercises developed primarily length and speed of the 
228	running stride, whereas the long jumping exercises largely increased maximum running speed and speed-strength 
229	endurance. The combination of short and long jumping cxerciscs led to a summation of their separate training 
230	effects and the development of speed-strength abilities which arc specific to sprinters.
231	Figure 5.12 Decrease in sprint times for three groups of athletes over various distances after 8 months of training. LS = low start, SS 
232	= standing start. (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
233	Under natural training conditions, three equivalent groups of jumpers of average qualification were used to 
234	compare the effectiveness of different systems of strength training (Fig 5.13). All of the groups used special 
235	jumping exercises in the first stage of the preparation period. Groups 2 and 3 switched to barbell exercises in the 
236	second stage, while group 1 continued to do the jumping exercises. Group 3 began to use depth-jumps in the third 
237	sage while group 1 continued to do the jumping exercises and group 2 did the barbell exercises.
238	The special strength training indicators displayed a clear tendency to stabilise in groups 1 and 2 after the first 
239	and second stages respectively, and in group 1, even to decrease during the third stage. Thus, the sequential use of 
240	means with higher, specific training effects dearly produces a positive result. At the same time, the use of the 
241	same means, even with an increase in volume, not only does not produce a positive change, but decreases the 
242	existing level of special strength fitness (Verkhoshansky & Aganin, 1970).
243	Research with novices and athletes of average qualification leads us to make the following conclusions about 
244	the effectiveness of the variants studied for these athletes:
245	• The best results are obtained by consistently using those combinations or complexes o f means which 
246	produce the optimal training effect (e.g. as shown in Fig 5.13)
247	• A slightly smaller effect is obtained by the concurrent use of strength and speed-strength means in one 
248	training session or their sequential use in successive sessions
249	• Least effective is the sequence of strength followed by speed-strength means during the same session.
250	Figure 5.13 Dynamics of the control indicators for the three groups using different combinations of training methods (see the text). 
251	(Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
252	Tk following principles for the sequential use of training means over a given period emerge:
253	289
254	
255	######## PDF 301 (printed 290)
256	SUPERTRAJNINC
257	• Strength exercises should be done after speed-strength exercises in training
258	• Strong-acting plyometric methods should be done after strength exercises, but not before.
259	In another study (Fig 5.14), qualified athletes modelled different variants of weightlifting pre-competition training 
260	under laboratory conditions (Deniskin, 1976). A leg extension movement involving the lifting of a 1RM was used 
261	as a model, starting with an initial knee angle of 90°. The training effect o f the plyometric method (with depth- 
262	jumps) was investigated after a fust stage of intensive work with resistance, the purpose of which was to increase 
263	explosive strength. Only depth-jumps were used during the sccond and third stages. The necessity for having two 
264	such stages was dictated by the results of a preliminary investigation which showed that the rise in functional 
265	state achieved after one stage is unstable. The fourth stage served as a control and served only to test 
266	performance. The subjects were given a complete rest between stages to enhance supercompensation.
267	The experiment showed that the plyometric method produces an additional, significant increase in the level of 
268	explosive strength that was first attained with resistance training. This demonstrates the use of these means in 
269	two appropriate stages: the first stage, which improves explosive strength, and the second stage, which stabilises 
270	the level of special fitness. 
271	There was a significant increase in all the control indicators after a period of complete 
272	rest following the first and sccond stages. This emphasizes that rest may be used as a training means. This is not 
273	a paradox, because growth and maintenance processes take place predominantly during sleep and other forms of 
274	passive or activc rest.
275	Several researchers have studied the systematic use of special strength training by highly qualified athletes 
276	under various training conditions (Purvin, Deniskin, Khodykin). It was established that using electromuscular 
277	stimulation (ES) first, followed by plyometrics yielded a larger training effect than the use of these means in the 
278	reverse order. However, a significantly larger training effect was obtained by using them together during the same 
279	stage, when, for example, ES and plyomctrics are applied concurrently with heavy resistance exercises. When the 
280	training is not chiefly for strength, ES and plyometrics were observed to have the lowest effect during periods of 
281	complete or partial rest.
282	Figure 5.14 Results of an experiment showing changes in performance indicators with different combinations o f training, as explained 
283	in the accompanying text. Ss » starting strength, Se = explosive strength, Fmax = maximum force, and tmax 53 time taken to reach 
284	maximum force Fmax. 
285	D-Jumps refers to Depth Jumps. (Deniskin, 1976)
286	2 9 0
287	
288	######## PDF 302 (printed 291)
289	SUPERTRAINING
290	5.3.1 Interaction betw een Different Training Means
291	Special attention must be paid to the prescription of general heavy resistance exercises. They enable the athlete to 
292	reach the necessary level of absolute strength, to provide general physical conditioning and to train the 
293	neuromuscular system non-specifically. However, it is undesirable to use them extensively during specialised 
294	training phases, since they can diminish speed and explosiveness. High volume strength loads used after a phase 
295	of specialised jump training can substantially reduce the existing level of explosive strength (by as much as 30%).
296	Kotz has shown that prolonged, heavy workloads slow the contraction speed of trained muscles. More 
297	specifically, Filinov has established that excessively heavy strength loads diminish the force and speed of boxers’ 
298	punches, while Deniskin (1976) has found that prolonged use of high volume strength loads diminishes the power 
299	and speed of weightlifters, high jumpers and triple jumpers.
300	Thus, speed-strength and strength-speed ccasc to increase after a ccrtain volume of heavy strength training has 
301	been executed. Deniskin observed this phenomenon after 18 weeks (54 workouts) of strength training. Other 
302	studies have also noted the same phenomenon after 50-60 training sessions or approximately 12 weeks of training. 
303	This research shows that there arc certain volumes and durations of strength training that are essential for 
304	achieving an optimum training effect. Exceeding these optimal values renders any further increase in training 
305	volume not only unproductive, but detrimental to the athlete's preparation.
306	The rising standards of performance in sport has led to a general increase in the volume of strength training 
307	and technical preparation, especially in speed-strength sports. Throwers have sharply increased their quota of 
308	maximum distance throws and throws with heavier-than-normal implements, while jumpers have increased the 
309	number of jumps with a full approach run and jumps for maximum height. For example, discus throwers may 
310	execute as many as 100 throws in one workout and high jumpers perform as many as 80 jumps.
311	The demands on time caused by this increase in training volume usually compels one to prescribe physical 
312	conditioning and technical training concurrently. From the point o f view of the theoretically valid principles of 
313	coupled effects, unity o f skills and fitness qualities and unity ofphysical and technical training, this approach would 
314	appear to be fully warranted. These principles, in their most general form, express the interactive nature of the 
315	training process. In this sense this is correct.
316	However, in the context of the yearly training cycle or the training of highly qualified athletes, then a literal 
317	interpretation of this concept of unified training by the concurrent prescription of physical and technical training 
318	leads to serious error. Such a solution immediately contradicts the well-known need for the athlete to practise 
319	technical skills when he is fresh.
320	For instance, research by Verkhoshansky and colleagues has established that excessive maximum strength 
321	training can impair speed-strength and technical skill in boxers (Verkhoshansky, 1977). It can also lead to a 
322	deterioration of several months' duration in the technique of weightlifters and javelin throwers. Other studies have 
323	shown that heavy training loads reduce one's ability to control movements, primarily of their most complex 
324	technical phases. The negative influence of heavy strength training on sports technique may be due substantially 
325	to deterioration of the speed-strength qualities of the neuromuscular system.
326	With the widespread, almost mandatory use of supplementary strength training in most sports, it is 
327	surprising that research such as that quoted above has not stimulated more extensive work to investigate the 
328	practical application of strength training in sport. In this regard, it is disturbing to note the minimally varying 
329	composition of popular training means and the rubber-stamp way in which they are applied in short-term and 
330	long-term training. Virtually the only factors that change are the load and overall volume. This highlights the need 
331	for developing a clearer methodology for structuring sport-specific strength training programmes and applying 
332	existing research findings more competently. In general, an effective system of using the means of special strength 
333	training may be devised in the way discussed in the following sections of this chapter and in Chapter 6.
334	5.3.2 A Sequential System of Training Means
335	The development of specific motor abilities from the level of performance of the average healthy person to a high 
336	degree of proficiency occurs in a specific pattern. Because of this pattern, it is necessary to sequentially improve 
337	the functioning of those systems and physiological mechanisms which are crucial for developing a specific motor 
338	ability.
339	291
340	
341	######## PDF 303 (printed 292)
342	SUPERTRAINING
343	Progressive functional changes in some systems act as prerequisites for improving the performance of other 
344	systems which limit development of the required motor abilities. It is easy to understand that the given response 
345	is produced only if the conditioning process is organised so as to produce suitable conditions which efficiently 
346	integrate the use of all means with different training effects.
347	It is known that, in order to steadily increase the body’s special work capacity, the means used should elicit a 
348	definite training effect, but its magnitude should correspond to the body's current level of specific fitness and 
349	increase in conjunction with the latter. Despite the logic of this principle, it is nevertheless not always practical 
350	to achieve. Very often the means are selected on the spur of the moment without considering their precise training 
351	effect and often on the basis of what is currently fashionable or subjectively preferred. For instance, means which 
352	are highly effective during more advanced stages of training may be used inappropriately during the early stages of 
353	the yearly cycle or in the beginning stages of multi-year training.
354	The repertoire of means is usually extremely limited and is repeated in much the same way from year to year. 
355	This is not a general trend but a fairly typical occurrence, which reveals that even well-known and theoretical 
356	principles of major significance are consciously or unconsciously ignored. Hence, the necessity becomes obvious 
357	for devising a scheme for sequentially introducing means of gradually greater training effect into training.
358	Specificity becomes more relevant to one's state of fitness as sports proficiency increases. At the same time, 
359	the role of the means used to develop trainability grows. Introduction of the means should be carefully timed and 
360	the contents of future training should be based entirely on the preceding stages. These means should be novel, so 
361	as to promote a greater training effect by compelling the adaptive processes to transcend any performance 
362	plateau.
363	Research has investigated changing the special training means only once or twice during the period of study. 
364	However, suitable variations for the systematic use of means with greater training effects involve multiple 
365	changes. Consequently, the logical organisation of training loads, as exemplified by the conjugate sequence system 
366	of special strength training needs to be examined. This is done in the next section.
367	5.3.3 The Conjugate Sequence System of Training Means
368	In the training of highly qualified athletes it always becomes necessary to raise the developmental level of any of 
369	the basic qualities o f the motor system which may be limiting improvement of the specific motor abilities. A 
370	logical solution would appear to be the introduction of a particular means capable of eliminating this insufficiency. 
371	However, this measure, which displays a very low probability of transferring specific motor abilities to the given 
372	sporting activity, is not very effective. If a specially sequenced system, known as the conjugate sequence system, 
373	is regularly used in training, then the likelihood that such situations will arise is minimised and the situation will 
374	rapidly improve (Verkhoshansky, 1978).
375	There are essentially two main systems of organising long term training: the concurrent system and the 
376	conjugate sequence system. The concurrent system involves the parallel training of several motor abilities, such as 
377	strength, speed and endurance, over the same period, with the intention of producing multi-faceted development 
378	of physical fitness. Although research has corroborated the effectiveness o f this system, the subjects used in 
379	these studies were generally conducted on athletes o f lower qualification. While the negative influence of the 
380	complex system is not apparent with less advanced athletes, it becomes very noticeable with elite athletes, in 
381	whom it produces only average results. To evoke a more powerful training effect in athletes who have already 
382	accommodated to high levels of stimulation, it becomes necessary to impose intense phases o f uni-directional 
383	loading on the body. This is precisely the purpose of the conjugate sequence system.
384	The conjugate sequence system (sometimes translated from the Russian as the coupled successive system) 
385	involves successively introducing into the training programme separate, specific means, each of which has a 
386	progressively stronger training effect, and coupling them sequentially to create favourable conditions for eliciting 
387	the cumulative effect of all the training loads. The conjugate sequence use of unidirectional means, integrated by 
388	separately developing individual, specific motor abilities (e.g. strength, speed and strength-endurance), can be an 
389	invaluable method of organising special strength training for more advanced athletes. Usually, it involves training a 
390	carefully chosen sequence of specific motor abilities, each of which is confined largely to a given period, a scheme 
391	that saves time and energy. It is appropriate to use concentrated loading primarily for enhancing the effectiveness 
392	of the SPP (Special Physical Preparation) phase, and for this, one may use loading of any primary emphasis.

437	Unidirectional emphasis on qualities such as strength or endurance may be used not only in individual worko 
438	but also during each microcycle (Kudelin, 1980; Budokho et al, 1978; Mironenko, 1980). Research has sho 
439	that unidirectional training over periods as long as 4-12 weeks can be very effective, especially if the intensity is 
440	gradually increased for each form of loading in the given cycle. Moreover, the effectiveness of the conjugate 
441	sequence system with advanced athletes is such that the training volume over a macrocycle can be reduced by as 
442	much as 20%, a phenomenon referred to as the acceleration o f specific adaptation (see 5.4.2).
443	However, it must be noted that unidirectional loading is effective only if one uses a diverse complcx of means 
444	with a single primary emphasis, together with a variety of training methods (Fedorova et al, 1975; Platonov &. 
445	Monograov, 1977; Verkhoshansky, 1977). Furthermore, an important condition for implementing concentrated 
446	loading is the relatively low intensity of the means, sincc the frequent use of these means already intensifies the 
447	training. In this context, the loading may be considered concentrated if its volume in the month in which it is 
448	applied constitutes 23-25% of the general volume for the year.
449	The system is not without its dangers, since concentrated loading is very stressful and, besides increasing the 
450	potential for overtraining, it can decrease motor qualities such as speed-strength. After a phase of emphasis on 
451	heavy strength training, there may be an increase in muscle stiffness and a loss of explosive strength, sporting skill 
452	or speed. Since the conjugate sequence system is based on exploitation of the delayed training effect, a diminished 
453	loading and restorative period has to be observed after a given concentrated loading phase to allow the body to 
454	supercompensate to the desired level o f preparedness. The gains elicited, for instance, by 4-8 week concentrated 
455	blocks of strength, speed-strength or speed training, may occur most commonly after a latency period of 1-3 
456	weeks, so it is essential for the athlete not to lose patience and hasten into the next concentrated phase without 
457	adequate restoration. Not only does premature imposition of concentrated loading suppress the delayed training 
458	effect of the previous stage, but it also lowers the effectiveness of future training.
459	5.4 The Principal Aims of Special S trength Training
460	During the initial stages of training the body reacts to any stimulus with all of its survival mcchanisms and motor 
461	abilities. As a result of this general adaptation response, the specific training effects which enhance working 
462	potential are not produced. Characteristically, there is a relatively high correlation between the various motor 
463	abilities and the development of even those abilities which are not directly implicated. The transfer of fitness is 
464	very distinct here.
465	As sporting proficiency grows, so the adaptation response becomes more selective. Functional adaptation is 
466	confined primarily to those systems which are the most active and develops in those directions which art 
467	determined by the specific components of the training stimulus. The close connection between separate motor 
468	abilities tends to diminish during the stage of high sports proficiency, the rate of development o f motor abilities 
469	which are not the direct object of training slows down, and the transfer phenomenon is not displayed as sharply 
470	as before. Thus, the direction of progress is determined entirely by the specific components of the training 
471	stimulus. Since sport achievements at the high levels of sports proficiency are produced by a complex of specific 
472	motor abilities, the regime of the means used should contain an optimal combination of specific training means.
473	It is now appropriate to formulate a set of general principles for organising special strength training, based on 
474	the specific characteristics of physical training and the long-term dynamics of the STS (Sports Training Process). 
475	In general, they express the chief ways o f exploiting these characteristics and form the foundation of a new 
476	system of sport training, although they do not exclude all of the traditional principles and rules. These principles 
477	are:
478	• Converging the partial effects of strength training means
479	• Accelerating specific adaptation
480	• Specific correspondence of the training effect
481	• Maintaining the strength training effect.
482	5.4.1 Converging the Partial E ffects of Strength Training Means
483	The principle of converging the partial effects o f strength training means is fundamental to the long-term 
484	organisation of strength training. It is achieved by the convergence of all the different partial training effects, i.e. 
485	the gradual convergence of their cumulative training effect to those important specific characteristics which are 
486	essential to the functioning of the body in a particular sport.

491	During the initial stages of the sports training process (STP) the tasks which determine the diversity of the 
492	training means are far apart. They are loosely connected only by the long-term plan of the STP and implied by 
493	that training programme which takes into account the characteristics of producing a specific type of fitness for a 
494	given sport.
495	In particular, this occurs by adaptation to the motor regime required by the sport, i.e. its specialisation is 
496	firstly according to ability (but not to the physiological system) and is not related to the motor pattern (see 2.2.3). 
497	At the same time, training of the body to improve performance involves enhancing its functional abilities and 
498	raising its working potential.
499	As the STP advances, the training effects of the means begin to converge according to their specificity. In this 
500	respect, the functional characteristics demanded by the sport determine the requirements of the special strength 
501	training, while the level of special fitness determines the progress of the STP as a whole.
502	Thus, at the high level of sports mastery the special strength training converges towards the specific character 
503	of the motor regime of the given exercise and its specific motor pattern. However, the criterion of successful 
504	convergence is the closeness of correspondence of the training effect to the performance characteristics of the 
505	given sport. As training progresses, the effect of the specific training means exceeds the required degree of 
506	closeness, while the general training means more strongly reflect the specifics of the special exercise. At this stage, 
507	there is a close interrelation between all components which constitute the STP. The correspondence between each 
508	of the components is reflected in the growth of sporting proficiency, the latter being determined by the body's 
509	level of special fitness and the athlete’s ability to attain his full motor potential.
510	This process is illustrated in Figure 5.16. During the STP the characteristics of the key motor ability M 
511	gradually move closer to the working pattern of the motor apparatus in sport A. At the same time the complex of 
512	individual motor abilities determining the key motor ability (i.e. M I, M2, M3) correspond more closely to the 
513	specifics of the key motor ability.
514	This concept has already been studied regarding early specialisation by youngsters (Verkhoshansky, 1963, 
515	1972). Since this question is directly connected with the initial stages of the STP, particular consideration was 
516	given to the advisability of early specialisation, not in the specific type of sport, but in the specific motor regime 
517	involved. In other words, orientation of the child to the sport and physical training with the sports means docs 
518	not begin with specialised exercise to achieve competitive performance standards (which can easily lead to forced 
519	training). Instead, it begins with systematic management of the functional perfecting of the body.

538	5.4.2 Acceleration of Specific Adaptation
539	The principle of accelerating specific adaptation emphasizes the key role of spccial strength training as the 
540	foundation for developing sports proficiency, with particular reference to its organisation over a long period. The 
541	idea is that specific adaptation should be accelerated by advancing the stage when maximum sports proficiency is 
542	expected to be produced by the current training regime. 
543	In practice this means that the task of functional 
544	specialisation should be based on accurate modelling of all aspects of the motor activity. The requirements of this 
545	specialisation are then presented to the body in a specific sequence during the STP (Sports Training Process) in 
546	order to accelerate adaptation.
547	Thus, the successful acceleration of specific adaptation depends on anticipating any conditions which may 
548	delay the subsequent course of the STP. This ensures the steady progress o f the STP, except when physical 
549	fitness lags due to unforeseen circumstances such as adaptational idiosyncrasies, illness or injury. Even then, a 
550	contingency plan should always be available to maintain the fitness level of those systems which can still be 
551	exercised.
552	The achievement of accelerated adaptation necessitates using statistical data which reflect the basic trends in 
553	the dynamics of the athlete's specific motor abilities in the given sport (sec 2.2.3), where the athlete's existing level 
554	of special physical fitness is carefully taken into account. This accelerated adaptation may be achieved by 
555	controlling the post-training supercompensatory phases by using the conjugate sequence method of training, by 
556	the heterochronicity principle of superimposed cycles of training the different components of fitness, by 
557	converging the partial effects of the training means, or by correctly periodised full or partial restoration after 
558	training (see 8.5).
559	Specialised means of strength training selected to take into account the specific movements of the given sport 
560	and the participant's existing level of fitness produce a timely and substantial increase in relative and starting 
561	strength, significantly exceeding the average indices typical of the training of that type of athlete. It should also be 
562	pointed out that the use of complex, novel means of strength training enable highly qualified athletes to avoid the 
563	typically slow rate of increase in starting strength.
564	5.4.3 Specific Correspondence of the Training Effect
565	The principle of specific correspondence points to the need for correspondence between the general effect of the 
566	strength work and the specific character of the motor regime of the given sport. This is achieved on the basis of 
567	systematically organising means so that the resulting cumulative effect fully establishes the special strength 
568	fitness required at the current stage of the sports training process.
569	The practical realisation of this aim should be based upon the following scheme of the functional 
570	specialisation of the body in the sports training process (Fig 5.17). Along with the body's general adaptation 
571	response, it selectively reacts to the dominant motor regime and movement pattern.
572	This causes local, functional improvement in the fitness qualities of the kinematic chain's motor system 
573	(specialisation o f systems) and develops qualities which are appropriate to the motor skills of the sport 
574	(.specialisation o f ability), as was discussed earlier (2.2.4). Subsequently, a definitive, more precise structure of the 
575	key muscle groups and the structure of their functional integration occurs, as well as the efficient development of 
576	the necessary specific motor abilities. Thus, specific correspondence of the training effect is based on the 
577	following tasks:
578	• Timeous development of the required level of special strength fitness
579	• Elimination, where necessary, of heterochronological stages which were initially suitable for the intense 
580	functional specialisation of the key muscle groups
581	• Elimination of any lag in the development of strength fitness of individual muscle groups
582	• Intensifying the development of the essential strength abilities during the stage of advanced sports mastery.

616	5.5 Cross Training in Sport
617	In the West, the term cross training refers to using relevant secondary sports to augment the training effect 
618	produced in an athlete's primary sport. 
619	It has been applied for some years to training which involves performing 
620	several sports daily or weekly within the same training programme. Thus, a supplementary fitness programme 
621	which incorporates gymnasium exercises, aerobics, cycling and swimming is popularly called 'cross training'. 
622	Typically, some exercises or sports are done on one day, others on another day.
623	In planning this type of training, it is important to recall the two basic ways of combining training: concurrent 
624	and sequential (see 5.3). Thus, cross training may involve supplementary activities being prescribed concurrently 
625	with the athlete's main sport on the same day or during the same training phase or in a definite sequence where 
626	one supplementary activity gives way to another and finally to the main sport over a given period. The design of 
627	any cross-training programme, therefore, necessitates applying a thorough knowledge of factors such as the 
628	interaction between activities of different primary emphasis, the influence of short- and long-term after-effects of 
629	training, supercompensation, the specificity of training, pcriodisation and restoration, topics which are covered 
630	elsewhere in this text.
631	In Russia and Eastern Europe, the prescription of adjunct means of physical preparation does not simply 
632	focus primarily on the type of sport used, but rather on the relationship between the motor and fitness qualities 
633	in the supplementary activities and the primary sport. This involves the qualitative and quantitative modelling of 
634	each sport involved so as to ensure that the supplementary sports do not impair performance in the primary 
635	sport (see Ch 6). It is inadequate, for example, to state that track-and-field athletics, rugby or American football 
636	require the development of strength, so that heavy weight training must constitute appropriate cross training. 
637	Earlier in this text, we have stressed the importance of defining the different types of strength and their 
638	development, so it should be obvious that this simplistic approach can offer little more than short term progress.
639	For many years the Russians and Eastern Europeans have supplemented the training o f their competitive 
640	athletes with systematic supplementary training in other sports. For instance, Olympic weightlifters and field 
641	athletes have included volleyball or basketball in their overall training regimens. In the West, however, 'cross 
642	training' generally has not advanced scientifically much beyond the way in which it was used several decadcs ago, 
643	and the choice of combinations, durations, intensities and periodisation systems is often guesswork. 
644	Combinational training o f complementary sports or exercises can be valuable if prescribed scientifically, but 
645	detrimental if done randomly.
646	Certain sports are used in Russia and allied countries during the off-season, some during the early 
647	preparation phases, others during the competitive season, and still others as a means of recuperation or enhancing 
648	certain qualities such as fine motor control or explosiveness. These sports have not been chosen simply to add 
649	random variety to stagnating athletes; they have been periodised carefully into closely monitored long-term 
650	training programmes. Part of this supplementary training has even included phases of specialised electrical 
651	stimulation of the muscles or the central nervous system.
652	The Russians have consistently identified the most important fitness factors required by specific sports, 
653	then divided the sports training programme into a periodised model aimed at using supplementary activities

658	(General Physical Preparation) to assist in the transfer of skills in the Specific Physical Preparation phase which 
659	precedes the Competition phase (Ch 6).
660	The concept of cross training is sound under certain circumstances, provided the tendency to overtrain is 
661	resisted. 
662	Variety usually adds interest, ensures novelty of neuromuscular stimulation and can reduce the 
663	likelihood of stagnation, but the enthusiasm it engenders can cause the recent convert to raise the intensity or 
664	volume of training to inappropriately high levels and produce overtraining.
665	As discussed previously, combinations of predominantly cardiovascular activities such as regular distance 
666	running, cycling or swimming with weightlifting, rugby, or other strength sports may be counterproductive, since 
667	muscular endurance and cardiovascular fitness may be enhanced at the expense of strength, muscle mass and 
668	power. Some sports can actually interfere with the fitness components and neuromuscular patterns acquired in 
669	other sports. The maxim of regular variation in training has to be applied with intelligent circumspection.
670	Similarly, inappropriate weight training using largely bodybuilding techniques might be detrimental to the 
671	marathoner or endurance athlete, especially if it fails to increase functional relative strength. The shortage of 
672	adequately trained strength specialists in local gyms renders incorrect use of supplementary resistance training a 
673	real possibility for serious athletes.
674	The term cross training has actually been used for many years by physiologists to describe the phenomenon 
675	whereby training one limb can produce a training effect in the opposite limb. The training effect elicited in one 
676	(ipsilateral) limb by active exercise or even passive manipulation is transmitted by central nervous pathways to 
677	the opposite (contralateral) limb. Though the strengthening effect is not as great as in the actively trained limb, 
678	this 'cross training’ effect can occur and usefully be applied in cases where an individual cannot use one limb due 
679	to injury (Enoka, 1988).
680	In the interests of etymology (the study of word origins) and scientific exactitude, it would be preferable that 
681	the term cross training be applied as intended originally and that a term such as combinational training or 
682	complementary training be used to describe physical conditioning via several sports in a single programme. At 
683	present, confusion exists in employing the same term for defining two different concepts in exercise prescription.
684	Some authors have been swift to categorise certain sports as beneficial and others as detrimental as ’cross 
685	training' activities for specific sports. This restricted view, however, fails to take into account the fact that every 
686	sports training programme consists of distinct overlapping phases, each concentrating on developing and 
687	integrating different fitness qualities. For example, it is erroneous to label cross-country running as totally 
688	unsuitable for rugby or American football players. Although prolonged aerobic activity generally is inadvisable 
689	for use during the competitive season, it can have a place during the early off-season period, since it can improve 
690	peripheral vascularisation and recuperation after intense exercise. 
691	Similarly, weight training should not be 
692	dismissed from the training schedule of a distance runner, when it may be useful in strengthening certain muscles 
693	or enhancing local muscle endurance.
694	To employ cross training efficiently and appropriately, it is essential to understand sports modelling and 
695	some of the different models of periodisation devised by Matveyev, Vorobyev, Verkhoshansky, Bogdanov, 
696	Kuzwccov and others, each of whom has worked in the Russia or Eastern Europe with different types of athlete. 
697	Most of these models comprise a General Preparation Phase, a Specific Preparation Phase, Transition Phases, 
698	Stabilisation Phases, a Competition Phase, Conversion Phases, Maintenance Phases and Reconstruction Phases 
699	(Ch 6). Once these principles are understood, it becomes possible to select different secondary sports and 
700	activities to augment each different phase of training for the primary sport. 
701	In order to do so, one must 
702	understand precisely which fitness qualities (static strength, dynamic strength, power, dynamic flexibility, muscle 
703	endurance and so forth) are developed by the primary and the secondary supplementary sports.
704	In this respect, it is important to recall that sporting prowess involves specialisation by physiological system 
705	and specialisation by ability or skill (see 2.2.3 and 5.4.3). Therefore, any cross training programme must ensure 
706	that it enhances and does not compromise either of these processes.
707	Some of the secondary activities may be used either to enhance the training effects of the primary sports or to 
708	assist in recuperation and relaxation after specific training for the primary sport. 
709	In doing so, it is vital to 
710	recognise that attention has to be paid not only to the physical, but also the psychological, effects of the 
711	secondary activities.
712	For example, learning to push against maximal loads during the late off-season and early season can enhance 
713	the overall motivation of a rugby or football player in coping with high levels of physical and mental stress. 
714	Swimming can teach an athlete a great deal about breathing patterns, dancing and gymnastics about coordination

721	Since some form of weight or circuit training is very popular as a cross training activity, it is vital to point out 
722	that most machines used in fitness centres constrain one to move along fixed, two-dimensional paths and, if used 
723	regularly, can interfere with the three-dimensional neuromuscular patterns characteristic of all sport, under-utilise 
724	the postural muscles or create muscular imbalances between agonists and antagonists. Similarly, isokinetic 
725	rehabilitation machines do not develop the three-dimensional, eccentric, concentric and explosive muscle activation 
726	patterns needed in competitive sport. They should be used only for limited, specific applications during the 
727	earlier stages of general physical preparation or rehabilitation.
728	In planning any type of cross training activity, it is always relevant to ask the questions: Will this activity be 
729	directly beneficial to my sport ?, Will this activity be indirectly beneficial to my sport?. When will other activities be 
730	beneficial or detrimental to my sport? and Would the time be better spent training with sport specific exercises?
731	Cross training is currently highly attractive and popular among journalists and coaches, but its successful use 
732	is by no means as simple as implied by many personal trainers. As one of the more sophisticated concepts in 
733	sports preparation, it requires an extensive theoretical knowledge of all aspects of physical conditioning, years of 
734	practical experience in working with different athletes, and close collaboration with experts in different sports.

736	Circuit training has once again surged into prominence as a training modality in commercial gymnasia, largely 
737	because of the fads promoted in the USA in response to the regularly changing appetites o f the average non­
738	competitive fitness client. Both instructors and pupils are becoming bored with traditional aerobics classes, 
739	aerobic dance is often too complicated for the fast-fitness client or uncoordinated male, weight training is still 
740	struggling against public confusion of it with overdeveloped bodybuilding physiques, so circuit training is step­
741	ping in as the so-called 'new' method of fitness conditioning.
742	Circuit training is by no means a new concept. As it is defined today, it seems to have been formalised by R 
743	Morgan and G Adamson in 1953 at the University of Leeds in England as a system which would train several of 
744	the components of fitness simultaneously, rather than strength or cardiovascular endurance separately.
745	Actually, circuit training is really an extended form of'supersetting', which has been used by the bodybuilding 
746	fraternity for decades (see Ch 7). It is defined as a routine which requires one to alternate sets between two (ora 
747	small number of) different exercises. For instance, a typical superset might require you to do set 1 of a bench 
748	press, then set I of a squat, back to set 2 of the bench press, then set 2 of the squat, and so on until the specified 
749	number of sets has been completed for both exercises. A circuit simply extends the superset from two or a few ex­
750	ercises to a sequence of many exercises .
751	The term 'circuit' now refers to a collection of'stations', each station being an area or specific machine or 
752	weight at which a chosen exercise has to be performed for a certain time or number of repetitions. Successive 
753	stations characteristically require one to use a prescribed resistance machine, bicycle, mini-trampoline, skipping 
754	rope, barbell or free exercises such as pushups, situps or jumps.
755	The typical modem circuit requires one to move rapidly in a stipulated order from station to station through 
756	the circuit and repeat it for a set number of times, the intention being to develop strength, cardiovascular stamina, 
757	muscular endurance and flexibility. Frequently a timing system with an audible alarm is used to signal participants 
758	when they should hasten to the next station. In other systems, a certain number of repetitions is prescribed for 
759	each station. A much publicised feature is its claimed ability to develop all these fitness factors, while lowering 
760	percentage bodyfat and improving shape.
761	What is not widely appreciated is the fact that most instructors rely on the circuit training systems developed 
762	and advertised by the manufacturers of expensive specialised machines. Equipment salesmen, for obvious reasons, 
763	do not promote the fact that highly successful circuits can be set up without apparatus or with very cheap 
764	apparatus. Circuits can even be set up on sports fields, in parks, in corridors, in the aerobics class or in the 
765	swimming pool.
766	The Aims of Circuit Training
767	As recounted earlier, circuit training has been advertised as a highly successful system for developing all-round 
768	fitness. However, this claim is not accurate for the average commercial circuit, since research has shown that only

adaptation. The principle of gradual progressive overloading may, after a prolonged period of unvaried use, 
sometimes fail to improve strength or performance, as is commonly the case among elite athletes. 
In this 
situation, it may be necessary to disrupt the persistent state of stagnation by use of one of the following shock 
methods (see 7.1):
• plyometrics 
• forced repetitions
• supramaximal methods 
• electrical stimulation (macrostimulation)
• repeated single I RM training 
• restricted range maxima
• contrast methods 
• maximal eccentrics
The appropriate method, its timing and the duration of its use must be chosen with great care, since lack of 
progress may be due to overtraining rather than long-term stagnation. The use of any shock method under such 
circumstances is potentially harmful and definitely detrimental to performance. These methods arc generally 
unsuitable for novices and should only be employed by experienced athletes with a solid background of special 
strength training.
5.2.5 The D evelopm ent of Strength-Endurance
Strength-endurance involves the production of muscular tension without a decrease in efficiency over a long 
period. Strength-endurance, like explosive strength, has several forms, depending upon the motor pattern of the 
athletic activity, in particular the categories of dynamic and static endurance.
Dynamic strength-endurance is typical of exercises involving repetitive and significant muscular tension at a 
relatively slow speed of movement, as well as repeated cyclic or acyclic exercises requiring speed-strength. In the 
latter case we are referring to the specific endurance to execute special speed-strength and explosive work without 
adecrease in efficiency over a relatively long period. Static strength-endurance is typical of activities associated 
with the maintenance of maximal and near-maximal tension, as well as the moderate tension necessary for holding 
a specific posture (for example, in shooting or speed-skating).
The development of strength-endurance is an inherent characteristic and a fundamental principle of training 
for dev eloping general endurance. Training for strength-endurance is determined predominantly by:
1. The magnitude of the load
2. The tempo of movement
3. The duration of each movement and each phase of the movements
4. The rest interval between training sessions
5. The length of the training period
6. The initial levels of strength-cndurance of the athlete
7. The kinesiological structure of the movement
8. The relative involvement of static and dynamic strength-endurance.
Repetition work with weights 25-50% of IRM at a moderate tempo (from 60-120 repetitions/minute) is used for 
developing strength-endurance. The effectiveness of strength-endurance development, using equivalent weights 
and movement tempos, will be higher if the work is executed to complete fatigue, although work of shorter 
duration (60% of the maximal work capacity time) also will yield satisfactory results (Agolinsky, 1953; 
Korobkov, 1953; Monogarov, 1958; Diachkov, 1961).
Strength-endurance, like the other characteristics of muscular activity, is specific. However, the specificity 
of strength-endurance is expressed to a lesser degree than the specificity of speed, for example, while its carry­
over from one activity to another is greater. When the activity involves repetitively overcoming significant 
resistance (exceeding 75-80% of IRM), one cannot enhance endurance, since one becomes constrained to 
developing strength predominantly (Zatsiorsky, 1966).
This study by Zatsiorsky showed that isometric endurance increased 84% as a result of exercising 10 times a 
day for 5 weeks with the elbow flexors holding a 60% maximal contraction for as long as possible. Dynamic 
auiurance increased by 93% as a result of performing these arm curls with a weight of 60% of 1 RM at a rate of 
28repetitions per minute until it was impossible to increase the tempo further. At the same time, the ability to 
execute repetitive isometric contractions (60% of maximal strength for 5 seconds of tension and 2 seconds of rest) 
to failure increased by 219%. A similar experiment with 10 dynamic movements executed daily with maximal 
resistance for 5 weeks resulted in increases in both dynamic and static strength, but dynamic and static endurance

######## PDF 297 (printed 286)
SUPERTRAINING
remained almost unchanged (Hansen, 1963). This indicates that it is necessary to optimise the volume of work 
required to develop strength-endurance.
It has been established that an increase in strength-endurance contributes to improving endurance in distance 
runners, skiers and skaters (Popov, 1968; Nabatnikova, 1972; Mikhailov & Panov, 1975). However, it must be 
emphasized that the magnitude of the strength load used is different if, on the one hand, the key quality required 
is general endurance and, on the other hand, it is strength-endurance.
It should be noted that certain popular strength exercises such as running with a sack of sand weighing 25% of 
the subject's bodyweight, barbell pressing, squats, 'good mornings', and twisting with a barbell not only do not 
enhance, but to a certain degree, will even hinder the development of endurance in cyclic type exercises 
(Maisuradze, 1960). It some instances the increase in strength is associated with excessive muscle hypertrophy, 
which is a by-product of strength training. Endurance and hypertrophy do not increase simultaneously and there 
is no correlation between them (Maison & Broekcr, 1941; McMorris & Elkins, 1954).
The lack of a definite correlation between special strength and muscle mass in different sports where the key 
quality is endurance has been observed by several authors (Chistyakov, 1965; Chcmyaev, 1965; Nabatnikova, 
1972). This conccms primarily cyclic sports (middle distance running, skating and skiing). In other cases, for 
example, with gymnasts, a positive linear correlation (R = 0.77) is noticed between strength-endurance and 
relative strength (Zhalei, 1964). Therefore, in those cases where endurance is associated with the display of 
significant strength, some muscular hypertrophy does not negatively influence training results.
The general principles concerning the development of strength-endurance, which were discusscd earlier, arc 
applied differently in each specific case, depending on the characteristics of the sport, for example:
• During the preparatory period, skiers should exercise with weights which are up to 65% of 1RM, in 
combination with simulation exercises on a flat surface, as well as with movements on roller-skis 
(Chistyakov, 1965).
• Middle and long distance runners obtain good results from lifting a barbell of 55-60% of bodymass up to head 
level 8-10 times rhythmically, clean-and-jerks with various weights (60-85% of bodymass); jumps with 
kettlebells from a squat position (using about one-third of bodymass for 18-20 repetitions) and squats with 
55-60% of bodymass until complete fatigue (Likachycvskaya & Kovalchuk, 1963). Exercises with weights 
of 60-80% of 1RM for multiple repetitions, jumping and hard running are also recommended (Popov, 1966).
• Exercises with heavy weights (80-85% of 1RM), as well as medium and small weights are recommended for 
developing strength-endurance in skaters. Exercises with heavy loads are executed for several sets at a 
moderate tempo for 4-12 repetitions per set until the point of complete fatigue, with 2-4 minutes of rest 
between sets. Exercises with light and moderate weights are executed as rapidly as possible for 15-25 
repetitions per set, for 3-5 sets with rest intervals of 5-8 minutes (Mikhailov & Panov, 1975).
• Male rowers obtain good results with weights of 50-80% of 1 RM and female rowers with loads of 30-40% of 
1RM (Ulrich ct al, 1966). Significant improvement (up to 40% from initial levels) in strength-endurancehzs 
been noted in women rowers working with light weights (18-20kg) for many repetitions (Chumakova, 1964). 
Improvement is greater with these weights than with larger loads (35-50 kg) executed in sets of 2-3 
repetitions, and it is even greater (by 28%) than that produced by a combination of both methods.
It is necessary to increase the amount of weight and the number of repetitions as strength-endurance increases. 
The following method is recommended for skaters to develop strength-endurance in the legs: increasing the 
number of barbell squats by 20-30 each week (beginning with 50 squats per set and over a period of 2-3 months 
increasing this to 200-300 repetitions), then increasing the amount of weight and starting a new cycle of strength 
training, but beginning with a smaller number of squats (Mikhailov & Panov, 1975).
For developing strength-endurance it is always appropriate to strive to execute the work under demanding 
conditions, though with movements whose coordination and structure in space and time are close to those of the 
special exercise. For instance, a runner may run with a small parachute resisting him or pull a loaded sled in the 
preparatory phases (Popov, 1966). Similarly, gymnasts may use a heavy belt and vest (Zhilei, 1964) and rowers 
a spccial water-resistancc dcvice attached to the hull of the boat (Chuprun, 1966). In the case of the rowers. 
strength-endurance as measured by the number of pull-ups, the number of arm flexions in the prone position and 
the number of barbell presses in 30 seconds increased by 57.1%, 27.8% and 9.1%, respectively.
